latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Primary or clinically active cytomegalovirus replication in monocytes, endothelial cells, epithelial tissues, and reticuloendothelial organs; the upstream driver of viral DNAemia, fever, hepatitis, and occasional tissue-invasive complications.
Type I interferon, IL-6, TNF, and other antiviral inflammatory signals causing prolonged fever, chills, malaise, myalgia, headache, and modest acute-phase reactants.
Expansion of activated cytotoxic T cells responding to CMV antigen; produces absolute and relative lymphocytosis, atypical lymphocytes, mild neutropenia, and a mononucleosis-like blood picture.
Hepatic inflammation from CMV infection and antiviral lymphocytic infiltration, typically causing AST/ALT elevation with mild cholestatic enzymes and usually preserved synthetic function.
Reactive lymphoid and mononuclear-cell expansion in spleen, liver, and lymph nodes, producing splenomegaly more often than prominent tonsillitis or bulky lymphadenopathy.
Immune-mediated exanthem spectrum during acute CMV, ranging from maculopapular rash to erythema multiforme-like targetoid lesions.

Transition from mono-like viral syndrome into clinically important colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis decompensation, myocarditis, neurologic disease, or other organ-invasive CMV, especially with impaired cellular immunity.
Transient immune cytopenias associated with acute CMV, including neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and rarely severe autoimmune hemolysis or immune thrombocytopenia.

CMV endothelial activation, antiphospholipid-like immune effects, and inflammatory coagulation changes that can rarely produce venous thrombosis, arterial thrombosis, splenic infarction, or portal venous events.
Rare escalation of CMV immune activation into HLH-like hyperinflammation with persistent fever, cytopenias, high ferritin, liver injury, and high mortality risk if untreated.
Sustained asthenia and reduced exercise tolerance after acute fever and viremia improve, often lasting weeks to months after symptomatic CMV mononucleosis.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: CMV replication and antigen burden trigger innate antiviral cytokines that drive fever and systemic symptoms.
CMV antigen presentation drives expansion of reactive CD8 T cells, the hematologic substrate of the mono-like syndrome.
Active CMV replication produces measurable blood CMV DNA.
Primary or recent CMV infection induces CMV IgM, although interpretation depends on avidity, seroconversion, and clinical context.
Pyrogenic cytokines produce prolonged intermittent or continuous fever, often the dominant symptom.
CMV mono-like illness often presents after days to weeks of fever rather than abrupt pharyngitis.
Antiviral cytokine sickness behavior causes malaise and fatigue.
Intermittent fever can produce chills or rigors during the symptomatic viral phase.
Systemic antiviral inflammation commonly causes myalgia.
Fever and antiviral cytokines commonly produce headache.
IL-6-dominant acute-phase signaling raises CRP, usually less dramatically than bacterial sepsis.
Reactive cytotoxic T-cell expansion produces absolute lymphocytosis.
Activated T cells appear as atypical lymphocytes on smear.
The lymphocyte expansion can raise total WBC; the degree is much higher in selected post-splenectomy cases.
Relative and sometimes absolute neutropenia is part of the mono-like blood picture.
Activated mononuclear cells expand reticuloendothelial tissues, especially spleen and liver.
CMV hepatitis raises AST, sometimes markedly.
CMV hepatitis raises ALT, often higher than AST in uncomplicated hepatitis.
CMV hepatitis may have a mild cholestatic component with alkaline phosphatase elevation.
Most cases keep bilirubin normal or only mildly elevated; higher bilirubin suggests severe hepatitis or cholestasis.
Fulminant hepatitis is rare but arises from severe CMV hepatic injury, especially with immune compromise.
Reticuloendothelial activation produces splenomegaly, often demonstrable on ultrasound or CT.
Hepatic reticuloendothelial activation can produce hepatomegaly in a subset of cases.
Lymphadenopathy can occur but is usually less prominent than fever, fatigue, hepatitis, and splenomegaly.
When lymphadenopathy is present, severity tracks reticuloendothelial activity.
Splenomegaly creates the structural substrate for splenic rupture after trauma or strenuous activity.
CMV can trigger heterogeneous cutaneous eruptions during the mono-like syndrome.
Targetoid erythema multiforme-like lesions are a recognized but uncommon CMV-associated rash pattern.
CMV gastrointestinal involvement or hepatitis can produce abdominal pain.
CMV gastrointestinal involvement can produce diarrhea even when the initial syndrome resembles mononucleosis.
CMV pneumonitis is uncommon in immunocompetent hosts but occurs with impaired cellular immunity or severe disease.
Higher organ-invasive activity increases the event hazard for clinically significant CMV organ disease.
Immune hemolysis or inflammatory marrow effects can reduce hemoglobin in complicated CMV.
CMV can cause mild thrombocytopenia and rarely severe immune thrombocytopenia.
Endothelial activation and prothrombotic immune changes create rare CMV-associated venous or arterial thrombosis.
Splenic infarction is a rare CMV complication linked to splenic enlargement and prothrombotic activity.
Persistent CMV antigenic stimulation can rarely trigger HLH-like hyperinflammation.
Convalescent immune activation sustains fatigue after fever and viral load improve.
Fulminant hepatic failure is one of the main life-threatening CMV complications in this leaf.
Severe tissue-invasive disease drives hospitalization, organ failure, and mortality risk.
CMV-associated HLH is rare but high-risk and requires urgent treatment.
Splenic rupture can cause abrupt hemorrhagic shock.

History of prolonged or intermittent fever, commonly one to several weeks before diagnosis.
Mild fever-related tachycardia may occur; shock physiology is not typical unless severe complications or another disease is present.
Chills or rigors can accompany intermittent CMV fever but are not usually septic-shock intensity.
Often normal to moderately elevated from lymphocytosis; very high values are most compatible with special contexts such as post-splenectomy T-cell expansion.
Reactive absolute lymphocytosis is a central mono-like feature.
Reactive atypical lymphocytes can be present but may be less striking than in classic heterophile-positive mononucleosis.
Relative or absolute neutropenia may accompany the lymphocyte-predominant blood picture.
Usually preserved; mild anemia can occur with inflammation or immune cytopenia.
Usually normal or mildly reduced; severe thrombocytopenia indicates an immune complication or another process.
Usually modestly elevated; very high CRP should prompt evaluation for bacterial infection, inflammatory disease, or tissue-invasive complications.
May rise with lymphocyte turnover, hepatitis, or tissue injury.
Commonly elevated from CMV hepatitis, usually without liver failure.
Commonly elevated from CMV hepatitis and can reach several hundred U/L.
Mild cholestatic enzyme elevation may occur with CMV hepatitis.
Usually normal or mildly elevated; jaundice or high bilirubin suggests severe hepatitis, cholestasis, or another diagnosis.
Usually not directly affected in uncomplicated CMV mono-like illness; important for antiviral dosing and toxicity interpretation.
Absent or mild in most CMV mono-like illness; prominent exudative pharyngitis should reduce specificity for this leaf.
Tonsillar exudate is generally absent; high values are not typical for CMV mono-like illness.
Lymphadenopathy may occur but is commonly absent or mild.
Severity or extent of lymphadenopathy conditional on lymphadenopathy being present.
Splenomegaly is a common imaging or exam correlate of reticuloendothelial activation.
Hepatomegaly may accompany CMV hepatitis but is less consistent than transaminase elevation.
Cutaneous manifestations occur in a subset and are heterogeneous.
Targetoid or annular erythema multiforme-like rash pattern conditional on rash being present.
Headache can occur with the febrile viral syndrome.
Myalgia is common in the systemic viral phase.
Fatigue and malaise are prominent during acute illness and may persist after fever resolves.
Abdominal pain reflects hepatitis, mesenteric/reticuloendothelial inflammation, or CMV gastrointestinal involvement.
Diarrhea can occur in severe CMV mononucleosis-like illness or CMV gastrointestinal involvement, especially with impaired host context.
Usually absent or mild unless pulmonary involvement or a separate respiratory infection is present.
Usually absent unless pulmonary involvement or another cardiopulmonary process is present.
Pulmonary infiltrates are usually absent in uncomplicated mono but can appear with CMV pneumonitis or severe systemic CMV disease.
Acute CMV serology axis; confirmatory in case files and not intended as ordinary presentation evidence.
Blood CMV DNA by PCR; confirmatory and useful for treatment monitoring, especially in severe or immunocompromised contexts.
Expected to remain negative or low in CMV mono-like illness; false positives are possible but not typical.
Rare but important event hazard when CMV hepatitis progresses to hepatic decompensation.
Low but nonzero hazard during splenomegaly, especially with trauma or strenuous activity.
Rare CMV-associated venous or arterial thrombosis hazard.
Rare splenic infarction hazard from CMV-associated prothrombotic activity and splenic involvement.
Hazard of clinically significant tissue-invasive CMV organ disease such as colitis, pneumonitis, severe hepatitis, myocarditis, or neurologic disease.
Rare HLH-like hyperinflammation hazard during severe CMV infection.
Composite host context for impaired CMV cellular immune control; use more specific context axes when available.
Renal impairment requiring dose adjustment or avoidance of nephrotoxic CMV antivirals.
Hepatic decompensation context, which changes hospitalization, monitoring, and antiviral risk-benefit.
Pregnancy or conception-planning context; modifies fetal-risk counseling and antiviral toxicity decisions.

Composite context for clinically meaningful susceptibility to secondary or opportunistic infection during CMV illness or antiviral-associated myelosuppression; use more specific infection-risk axes when available.

Lifespan outcome hazard for CMV mononucleosis-like illness; very low in uncomplicated immunocompetent disease and driven upward by tissue-invasive CMV, fulminant hepatitis, HLH, splenic rupture, thrombosis, or severe immunocompromise.
Oral thrush is a structured host-context clue for advanced cellular immunodeficiency or Candida overgrowth; it is not a disease-specific mechanism for this leaf.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and CRP share upstream cytokine drivers, though either may lag or be modest.
Reactive lymphocytosis and atypical lymphocytes usually rise together because both reflect activated T-cell expansion.
The mono-like differential is lymphocyte-predominant and may show relative or absolute neutropenia.
AST and ALT share hepatocellular injury drivers in CMV hepatitis.
CMV hepatitis may produce both hepatocellular and mild cholestatic enzyme abnormalities.
Rising bilirubin with CMV hepatitis suggests cholestasis or liver dysfunction and increases concern for decompensation.
Larger or symptomatic spleen increases rupture risk during the active mono-like phase.
Tissue-invasive CMV shifts prognosis from self-limited viral syndrome toward organ failure risk.
HLH-like hyperinflammation is a rare but high-mortality CMV complication.
Major thrombotic events can cause organ infarction, pulmonary embolism, stroke, or other severe outcomes.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Observation alone is less adequate when tissue-invasive CMV is likely.
Impaired cellular immunity increases risk of prolonged viremia and organ disease.

treatments.context_specific_role: Default management for uncomplicated immunocompetent CMV mono-like illness with stable liver function and no organ-invasive features.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Dose reduction or avoidance is needed with hepatic decompensation or heavy alcohol use.

side_effects.interpretation: Dose-related hepatotoxicity risk, especially if excessive dosing occurs during CMV hepatitis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Symptom control for fever, headache, and myalgia; monitor dose carefully when transaminases are high.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antiviral benefit is strongest when severe, persistent, or tissue-invasive CMV is present.
Impaired cellular immunity reduces spontaneous clearance and increases the value of antiviral therapy.
Baseline neutropenia increases the risk of ganciclovir marrow toxicity.
Renal impairment requires dose adjustment and toxicity monitoring.

failure_modes: no net benefit in uncomplicated self-limited immunocompetent disease

side_effects.interpretation: Renal dosing and toxicity monitoring context

treatments.context_specific_role: IV antiviral for severe, persistent, hospitalized, immunocompromised, or tissue-invasive CMV disease; not routine for uncomplicated stable immunocompetent mono-like illness.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Oral therapy is useful when treatment is needed and enteral absorption is reliable.
Teratogenicity and reproductive toxicity require specialist risk-benefit assessment.

failure_modes: reduced absorption in severe colitis or vomiting
treatments.context_specific_role: Oral antiviral option for selected severe or persistent CMV when treatment is justified and oral absorption is adequate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Foscarnet avoids ganciclovir marrow suppression and may be considered when neutropenia prevents ganciclovir.
Nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances make foscarnet difficult in renal impairment.

failure_modes: IV-only toxicity burden in self-limited disease
treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue antiviral for selected severe CMV when ganciclovir resistance or marrow toxicity limits first antivirals.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Steroids are useful only for severe immune cytopenias or inflammatory complications, not routine CMV fever.
Steroids may be part of HLH-directed therapy while antiviral and specialist therapy address the trigger.
Steroids can impair viral control and should be paired with antiviral therapy when severe CMV disease is active.

failure_modes: worsened CMV replication if used without antiviral coverage in severe active disease
treatments.context_specific_role: Reserved for severe immune cytopenias or HLH-like complications under specialist care; not for routine uncomplicated CMV mono-like illness.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Avoidance of contact sports and strenuous activity is most important when splenomegaly is present.

treatments.context_specific_role: Prevents trauma-associated splenic rupture while splenomegaly is active.

seronegative_susceptible.trajectory_modulation: Primary infection substrate; symptomatic mono-like illness is most coherent when the host was previously CMV-seronegative.

seropositive_past_infection.trajectory_modulation: Reactivation can occur but a classic mono-like syndrome is less likely without immune compromise.

childcare_or_close_contact_with_young_ch.trajectory_modulation: Young children shed CMV in saliva and urine for prolonged periods.

sexual_or_body_fluid_exposure.trajectory_modulation: Compatible exposure context modestly raises CMV prior without acting as confirmatory evidence.

recent_blood_transfusion.trajectory_modulation: Transfusion exposure can introduce CMV, especially in susceptible or asplenic hosts.

remote_splenectomy.trajectory_modulation: Asplenia or hyposplenia can increase severity of systemic viral presentations and distort leukocyte response; it is context, not a CMV subtype.

solid_organ_transplant.trajectory_modulation: Higher viral load, prolonged shedding, and tissue-invasive CMV risk; mono-like presentation may be incomplete.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Impaired cellular immunity permits higher CMV DNAemia.
Transplant immunosuppression strongly increases tissue-invasive CMV disease risk.

advanced_hiv_or_cd4_lymphopenia.trajectory_modulation: High risk for tissue-invasive disease such as retinitis, colitis, esophagitis, or pneumonitis rather than a pure mono-like syndrome.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Severe cellular immune deficiency greatly increases tissue-invasive CMV risk.

iatrogenic_immunosuppression.trajectory_modulation: Steroids, chemotherapy, biologics, or antimetabolites can prolong viremia and increase tissue-invasive complications.

no_known_immunocompromise.trajectory_modulation: Classic CMV mononucleosis-like illness is most often recognized in immunocompetent adults; absence of known cellular immunosuppression favors a mono-like syndrome over tissue-invasive CMV.

pregnant_or_planning_pregnancy.trajectory_modulation: Maternal symptoms may be mild, but fetal transmission risk makes diagnosis, counseling, and antiviral risk-benefit different from ordinary adult disease.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Pregnancy is a treatment-context modifier rather than a direct disease-severity axis.

renal_impairment.trajectory_modulation: Does not by itself explain CMV mono-like illness but strongly changes antiviral dosing and toxicity.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Renal impairment changes antiviral dosing and toxicity risk.

supportive_care: Observation without antiviral therapy for stable immunocompetent patients without organ-invasive disease, severe cytopenia, or hepatic decompensation.
Antipyretics and analgesics with careful acetaminophen dosing when transaminases are elevated.
Oral hydration, IV fluids if oral intake is poor, and avoidance of unnecessary prolonged antibacterial therapy once bacterial infection is not supported.
Repeat CBC with differential and liver enzymes until fever and hepatitis trend down.
CMV IgM, CMV IgG seroconversion or avidity, and blood CMV DNA are confirmatory/monitoring tests and should not be treated as ordinary presentation observations in case ranking.
Screen for immune compromise, pregnancy, and organ-invasive symptoms because these contexts change antiviral risk-benefit.
Avoid contact sports, abdominal trauma, and strenuous activity while splenomegaly is present or suspected.

Escalate urgently for persistent high fever with worsening cytopenias, rising ferritin, coagulopathy, jaundice, encephalopathy, dyspnea, severe abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, or focal neurologic symptoms.

Use ganciclovir or valganciclovir only when severity, tissue-invasive disease, prolonged uncontrolled symptoms, or host immune context makes antiviral benefit outweigh marrow, renal, reproductive, and teratogenic toxicity.
Specialist input for pregnancy, transplant recipients, advanced HIV, severe hepatitis, suspected HLH, pneumonitis, colitis, myocarditis, neurologic CMV, or antiviral resistance.
